title: attackers are evolving. so should WE!!!
excerpt: Attackers are using AI. That is not a good reason to replace the humans defending the network.
body:
yeah, that’s real. if you look at the latest from the google threat intelligence group (gtig), the reality is scary: threat actors aren’t playing around. they are scaling up fast, and the bar for entry has never been lower.

state actors are already using AI to hunt for vulnerabilities in embedded devices and routers. cybercriminals are using generative ai to spot high-level semantic logic flaws… like the recent zero-day 2FA bypass on an open-source admin tool that traditional static scanners completely missed. they are actively building autonomous malware like PROMPTSPY and polymorphic evasion tools just to bypass detection.

AI is a massive force multiplier for them.

so what are we doing about it? instead of stepping up, a lot of companies are trying to outsource their security entirely to ROBOTS!! they are laying off people to cut costs.

this is a massive mistake.

stripping away human talent to save on payroll is a mathematical failure. yes, ai is a great tool for defenders too,, google even uses agents like Big Sleep and CodeMender to find and fix vulnerabilities automatically. but ai cannot replicate the adversarial mindset and contextual reasoning of a dedicated privacy engineer or threat hunter. models might surface dormant logic errors, but human defenders are the ones who understand the architecture, adapt to novel threats, and actually protect the network.

we need human intuition augmented by ai, not an empty SOC run by a language model.

DEAR CTOs, INVEST IN YOUR SECURITY BEFORE IT IS TOO LATE.

hire more. the bar to hack has never been this low.
THERE ARE MORE THREAT ACTORS THAN EVER, and they have AI too.

title: Tracing a Kernel Panic: What Actually Happens When You Hit “Sleep”?
excerpt: What actually happens when you put a Linux machine to sleep? I followed a kernel panic to find out.
body:
Is it as simple as “Closing your eyes”? and what happens to RAM/VRAM?

Usually we don’t think about it.
We click a button, the screens go black, the fans spin down, and we walk away. But underneath, a massive, high-stakes logistical operation is happening in milliseconds.

Here is the mechanical truth: your system RAM stays powered on, holding your operating system and apps in a suspended state. But your GPU? A modern graphics card has massive amounts of Video RAM (VRAM). To safely enter S3 sleep mode, the graphics driver has to quickly evacuate that entire VRAM payload and dump it directly into your system RAM.

It is called Buffer Eviction.
And yesterday, that exact process completely locked up my machine.

The Problem:

I run a highly optimized Linux Fedora setup on a Ryzen ZEN 5 and an AMD RDNA4 GPU.

I was running alot of processes taking alot of RAM and VRAM at the same time -imagine running VMs and Local LLMs- , I hit the sleep button, and…
the system hard-froze.
The monitors locked up.
The keyboard died.
I had to force-power the machine off, instantly losing my terminal sessions, my code, and my progress.

Random hardware freezes are a direct threat to a your workflow.
I needed to know exactly why the system failed.

Under the Hood:

I started Investigation Instead of guessing, I pulled the system logs from the crashed boot using journalctl.

The kernel was screaming two specific errors right before it died:
kernel: [TTM] Buffer eviction failed
kernel: amdgpu 0000:03:00.0: PM: device_prepare(): pci_pm_prepare returns -12

In the Linux kernel, Error -12 translates to -ENOMEM (No Memory).

The math of the crash became obvious. I was pushing my memory hard. Fedora uses zram by default, which acts as a swap space by compressing data inside your physical RAM.

When I hit Sleep, the RDNA4 GPU tried to dump gigabytes of VRAM into my system memory. But my RAM was nearly full, and the zram had nowhere to expand. The hardware literally ran out of microscopic space, the buffer eviction failed, the kernel panicked, and the entire system locked up.

The Fix:

The goal was to engineer a bypass for the memory bottleneck without breaking the speed of my current setup.

Using Btrfs, I allocated a dedicated 18GB physical swapfile directly on my SSD: sudo btrfs filesystem mkswapfile --size 18G /swapfile_18G

I locked it into the filesystem table. The logic is simple: zram continues to handle the lightning-fast, everyday memory compression. But when that massive GPU sleep-state dump happens and RAM maxes out, the system seamlessly spills the overflow into the 18GB safety net on the hard drive.

I tested it immediately. Maxed out the RAM, hit sleep, and the swapfile caught 3.5GB of overflow.
The system slept cleanly and woke up flawlessly.

The Lesson:

When building a complex system, you have to look at the entire board.

A GPU crash wasn’t actually a GPU problem; it was a file system and memory allocation bottleneck.
You can’t troubleshoot hardware in a vacuum.
Everything is interconnected.

Use the logs, find the mechanical truth, fix the root cause, and get back to building.

title: The Math of Success: If you are smart/hardworking, why aren’t you rich?
excerpt: Being smart and working hard matter. They just are not the entire equation.
body:
We’ve all heard the same advice from social media gurus:

“Sacrifice your 20s. Grind 100 hours a week. Sleep when you’re dead. If you aren’t rich, you just aren’t working hard enough man.”

I bought into this entirely. From age 18 to 20, I operated at absolute maximum capacity. I doubled down on health… hitting the gym daily in university-off months, and eating a hyper-strict diet… I spent every waking hour optimizing my tech stack, mastering Linux, and working as hard as I can.

I was playing the game at a 0.99 intensity level. And it worked, to an extent. I built incredible discipline and technical skills. But then, I stumbled upon a physics paper that completely shattered my worldview and changed how I will live the rest of my life.

The paper mathematically proves that extreme success isn’t about hard work. It’s almost entirely about luck.

Here is the mathematical truth about hustle culture, why I immediately dialed my life back to a sustainable pace at age 20, and how you can rig the game of life in your favor without burning out.

The Meritocracy Myth (The Talent vs. Luck Paper)

In 2018, physicists Pluchino, Biondo, and Rapisarda published a paper titled Talent vs Luck: The Role of Randomness in Success and Failure (arXiv:1802.07068).

They set out to solve a glaring mathematical paradox:

  • Human talent and effort follow a normal bell curve.
    The smartest or hardest-working person is maybe 2x or 3x more productive than the average person. Nobody is biologically capable of working 1,000 times harder.
  • Wealth and extreme success follow a power law (The 80/20 Pareto rule).
    A tiny fraction of people hold billions of times more wealth than the average person.

If inputs (talent/work) are linear, but outputs (wealth) are exponential, talent alone cannot explain the gap.

The Simulation

The researchers built a 40-year computer simulation where agents of varying “talent” (a catch-all term for intelligence, skill, and hard work) moved through a world encountering random events.

  • Green Events (Good Luck): If you hit one, your wealth doubles (compounding). However, you only catch it if your talent score is high enough… A talent level of 0.5 will catch 50% of the good events that he faces.
  • Red Events (Bad Luck): A market crash, a health crisis, a layoff. If you hit one, your wealth is cut in half. Crucially, your talent cannot protect you from this… It will hit you no matter what…

The Results: The wealthiest agents at the end of the 40 years were never the smartest or the hardest working. The peak earners were consistently mediocre people who experienced an uninterrupted streak of good luck and dodged all the red events.

Meanwhile, highly talented people who ground themselves to the bone frequently ended up broke simply because they encountered unavoidable, random “red events” that wiped out their compounding progress.

Why “Sacrificing Your 20s” is a Terrible Mathematical Bet

When you look at social media billionaires, you are looking at the Apex Anomaly: the 0.0001% of people who were highly talented and won the absolute lottery of uninterrupted good luck.

When you grind 100 hours a week, sacrifice your sleep, and destroy your social life, you are betting everything on becoming the Apex Anomaly. But Game Theory tells us this is a catastrophically stupid bet.
Why? Because you cannot control the “Red Events.”

You can sacrifice your entire youth to build a startup, reach a 0.99 talent level, and still get wiped out by a random economic collapse.
Even worse, by not resting, you dramatically increase the chances of triggering a self-inflicted red event: Burnout.

I realized that operating at a 0.99 intensity was mathematically reckless. I was volunteering for maximum downside (ruining my mental health) for a lottery ticket I couldn’t control.
So, at age 20, I stopped. I adopted a Minimax strategy: minimize my maximum possible loss, while leaving room for maximum possible gain.

I call it the Sustainable Life.

The Sustainable Life Protocol

To win in life, you don’t need to be a billionaire.
You need to ensure your capital never hits zero, protect your physical baseline, and stay outside long enough to get wet when it rains.

Here is the exact framework I operate on today:

1. The Baseline Rule (Protect the Floor)

Cover your survival expenses and other needs.

2. Maximize “Luck Surface Area” (Stop Grinding, Start Attracting)

Pray for luck, and at the same time remember that you can control where you stand when it rains.

Expand your Luck Surface Area (LSA) by:

  • Digitally: Put your work out into the world where a random “green event” (a recruiter, an investor, a collaborator) can trip over it.
  • Socially: Invest time in human networking. Most lucky events are handed out by other humans.

3. The Anti-Burnout Schedule

Here is what a mathematically optimized week looks like:

  • 9:00 AM — 5:00 PM: Secure the baseline capital safely.
  • +1 Hour/Day: Flexible time for passion projects and expanding your LSA. (If you hit a flow state, You keep going. If you are exhausted, stop).
  • Fridays: 100% Rest. Complete detachment from screens and productivity. This is mandatory to prevent the biological “red event” of burnout.
  • Saturdays: Deep tech/coding dives. Pure, unadulterated building with zero pressure to monetize.
  • Sundays: Back to 9–5.

The Final Verdict

You do need some hard work. You have to build enough discipline and skill (around a 0.5–0.7 talent score) to actually catch the lucky opportunities when they arrive.
You have to have a hard time at first to get to that baseline... 1–2 years are enough to boost you from 0.5 to 0.7 for example… depends.

But once you reach high competence (e.g. 0.7), sacrificing your life for a 1% increase in skill (e.g. 0.8 or 0.9) is a bad move in the chess board.

The gurus want you to believe life is a vending machine: put in 100 hours of suffering, get out a million dollars. The math proves life is not. The real winners aren’t the ones betting their life savings on one spin of the game.

The real winners are the ones who get a stable job, try to win small wins that they can affoard to lose, take Fridays off to hang out with their friends, and stay healthy.

If a lucky lightning bolt strikes, your net is wide open to catch it. And if it doesn’t? You have a great job, You are physically healthy, and You get to build what you love. In the worst-case scenario, You still win.

*Note: 0.5 -avg- talent score catches 50% of the good events… and so on.

title: Static Weights in a Dynamic World: The Case for “Artificial Information”
excerpt: A model can know a lot and still be working with yesterday's world. A few thoughts on that gap.
body:
It is Artificial Information, not Artificial Intelligence.

We need to stop confusing a massive database with a working mind.

We haven’t built a digital brain — we’ve built the world’s most efficient archive.

Here is why the “Intelligence” label is a lie:

1. The Static Trap

Biological intelligence is defined by adaptability. If you touch a hot stove, you rewire your neural pathways instantly. You learn.

AI is frozen in time.

Once a model is trained, its weights are static. If it makes a mistake, it will make that same mistake a thousand times until a human developer manually intervenes, curates data, and pushes an update.

That isn’t learning. That’s just software awaiting a patch.

2. Simulation vs. Reasoning

People point to models like o1 and say, “Look, it’s reasoning!”

It isn’t. It’s traversing a probability map of how humans have previously reasoned. It is retracing our footsteps, not forging a new path. It can emulate the process of logic, but without the intent or understanding behind it, it’s just a parrot with a better memory.

3. The Novelty Wall

Real intelligence applies old knowledge to completely new, unseen problems.

AI operates on precedent. It solves problems by identifying statistical correlations in its training data.

If an AI encounters a truly novel scenario,, one with zero correlation to the past,, it hallucinates or fails. It cannot derive first principles. It cannot “figure it out.”

We have democratized access to information on an incredible scale. That’s impressive enough.

But let’s be real about what this is:

Artificial Information.

Until a machine can rewrite its own code in response to a new stimulus without a human holding its hand, it’s just a glorified encyclopedia.

title: Stop Letting Your College Major Define You
excerpt: The major you chose at 18 is a starting point, not a life sentence.
body:
I had a task, which was “You have to speak to +100 freshmen to the IT college, give them ONE advice.”

It was a hard decision to filter out what is my most important advice to this specific type of audience, and it was this…

The major you chose at 18 is a starting point, not a life sentence.

At eighteen, we’re asked to choose a path that will supposedly define our careers.

We check a box: “Cybersecurity,” “Software Engineering,” “Data Science.” And just like that, an identity is assigned.

The problem? In a field as dynamic and interconnected as technology, this identity can quickly become a cage.

We see students build walls around that identity.

They focus only on their specialized courses, join clubs exclusive to their major, and follow a “roadmap” career path.

This tunnel vision is the fastest way to limit potential.

Tech, Tech, Tech…
That’s all it is, it is all inter-connected… literally.

Fellow CyberSecurity Student,,, You can’t protect what you don’t understand.
Fellow SWE Student, You can’t solve problems you don’t see.
And this list goes on for every major.

The major you chose at eighteen does not define your identity for the rest of your life.

The most valuable and successful professionals are not the ones who stay in their lane.

They are the ones who are curious enough to look over the fence, learn the language of other disciplines, and connect the dots.

Never, ever let your major be the limit of your ambition.

title: Reject ARM, Embrace x86.
excerpt: A slightly opinionated look at ARM, x86, and choosing hardware for what you actually need.
body:
Reject Modernity, Embrace Tradition.

When I first unboxed my new ARM laptop, I thought it was the end of an era.
This thin, silent machine was a monster.
The performance was incredible, the battery lasted forever.
“This is it,” I thought.
“I can do all my work on this.”

So I sold my x86 desktop.
Why be chained to a desk when I have this beast in my backpack?

That confidence lasted right up until the first time I needed a critical piece of software.
I went to the download page and saw it: appname.amd64.

“Wait… where’s the ARM64 version? Hello?”

No problem, I thought.
My monster machine can emulate it, right?

Right?

Technically, yes.
It “can” run it… at about 6% of native speed.
A task that should take seconds turned into a coffee break.
It was unusable.

So, I went out and bought an old x86 ThinkPad.

Now, my backpack contains two laptops.
One is a silent, modern that can’t run my essential tools.
The other is an “obsolete” workhorse that just works.

This taught me a hard lesson: There is no ARM machine today that can fully replace an x86 machine.
But there are plenty of x86 machines that can replace an ARM one.

My next machine will definitely be an x86 one, inshallah.
ONE… Not TWO.

They say a smart person learns from their mistakes.
A genius learns from others’.

Have you learned the lesson?

title: AI Bubble.
excerpt: Some thoughts on the AI hype, the money behind it, and what might actually last.
body:
AI.. AI.. AI…
Two characters that get repeated over and over again every day…

All of us have been impressed by the revolution of GPT 3.5 at 2022,,, like
“Wow I can speak to him directly????? an answer tailored to ME from HIM????? and HE CAN ANSWER SPECIFIC TOPICS TOO???”

Then GPT 4 came out at 2023,,, and it went like…
“WOW, I can send him photos now and he can very well analyze it without needing any text on it??? just like a human????”

Then the speech feature came out,,, and it went like
“WOW, I can speak to him just like speaking to a human??? with this natural voice????”

But now…
What else don’t we have already??
We already have everything we want from this tool.
What more can they add? Without it being too intrusive?
I don’t want an online chat-bot to read all of my browsing activities.
I don’t want an online chat-bot to see everything I see daily ( AI glasses ).
I don’t want an online chat-bot to hear every conversation I have.
I want privacy, it is a human right…
I want to USE the tool whenever I NEED, whenever I DECIDE to.

So I think both of us agree that We already got to the point where We have already achieved all of the normal wanted features.

Anything we add upon it is just an improvement to it, which doesn’t offer a big enough change to justify the overvalued state of the AI market at the current moment.

GPT-5 released this year, and honestly…
It didn’t manage to impress me more than the previous GPT-4o model.

People don’t care about numeric evaluation of things, People care about tangible improvements of things.

The photo speaks of it self.

title: You Should Quit Coffee,,, But Not Caffeine
excerpt: Coffee and caffeine are not the same conversation. Here is why I separate them.
body:

Get your caffeine, get your focus.

No brown teeth, no empty wallet, no microplastics.

TAILORED for YOU.
